Codex Vaeloria II: Armory of Relics and Bestiary
Ashfall Colossus
The Ashfall Colossus is a threat-rating 9 creature and a nocturnal ambusher. Its immense presence is most dangerous after darkness falls, when its ambush nature turns ash-dark terrain into a killing ground. The creature does not require open ground to exert its menace. Ruined approaches, ash-choked hollows, collapsed avenues, and other obscured terrain permit its mass to remain indistinct until withdrawal is no longer practical.
It appears as an enormous, ash-marked mass whose scale makes its approach feel like a moving ruin. Its outline is commonly perceived in fragments: a rising bulk beyond the dimness, a surface broken by ash, or a slow displacement of debris. Such impressions are sufficient for identification. Full observation is not required to establish the presence of the Ashfall Colossus.
Its demeanor embodies patient, crushing menace concealed beneath the night. It is not catalogued as a creature of sudden frenzy. The danger lies in concealment, timing, and the pressure imposed by its immense form. A watch that mistakes stillness for safety may discover the error only when the surrounding terrain has become a killing ground.
The Ashfall Colossus lairs in Embermarch. Records concerning its lair should be treated as operationally incomplete; the known designation establishes its region, not the security of any particular approach. Ash-dark terrain within Embermarch warrants heightened caution after darkness falls, particularly where visibility is reduced and the ground offers cover for an enormous mass.
The Ashfall Colossus was unleashed in The Purge of Blackport. This entry records that deployment as a fixed fact of the creature’s history. The circumstances of its release are not expanded here. Its appearance in that event confirms the strategic danger of directing such a creature into inhabited or contested ground, where its ambush nature and scale can transform existing ruin into an immediate hazard.
Field annotation: Do not classify the Ashfall Colossus by apparent motion alone. A moving ruin may be the creature itself; apparent stillness may indicate concealment. After darkness falls, ash-dark terrain is to be regarded as compromised until the creature’s absence is established.
Chalice of Ashdeep
The Chalice of Ashdeep is a reliquary forged in 323 AS. Its construction is recorded as having taken place at Marrowwell Abbey, in 323 AS. The object is presently housed in Crookgate Keep. These particulars establish its recognized provenance and current custody; no alternative place of forging or housing is entered in the relic rolls.
Its visual identity is that of a reliquary bearing the name Chalice of Ashdeep. The form is accordingly treated as ceremonial rather than utilitarian in classification. Descriptions of the vessel consistently preserve the distinction between its material body and its relic function: the former is observed, while the latter determines its formal entry in the armory register.
The Chalice of Ashdeep suggests a deep, ashen solemnity. This demeanor is neither recorded as a spoken manifestation nor assigned a separate supernatural effect. It is the accepted interpretive designation for the impression produced by the artifact’s appearance and presence. Scribes are instructed to retain this wording when preparing inventories, custody reports, or attunement notices.
Attunement to the Chalice of Ashdeep costs 27. The cost is recorded without additional qualification. No lesser or greater attunement category is supplied in the canonical register.
The relic’s record is therefore compact but exact: Chalice of Ashdeep is an artifact of class reliquary; Chalice of Ashdeep was forged in 323 AS; Chalice of Ashdeep was forged at Marrowwell Abbey in 323 AS; and Chalice of Ashdeep is housed in Crookgate Keep. Its attunement cost is 27. Its recognized demeanor remains one of deep, ashen solemnity.
Cinder Shrike
Identification
The Cinder Shrike is a threat of extreme severity. It bears a shrike-like silhouette, but its aspect is blackened and ember-dusted, as though shaped from cinder and marked by the residue of a spent fire. At distance, the form may be mistaken for a motionless fragment of ruin. This resemblance is unreliable. The creature’s outline is most often registered only after it has moved.
Its demeanor is silent, watchful, and violently sudden. No dependable warning cry, footfall, or preparatory display is recorded in the standard account. Its stillness should not be interpreted as torpor. The Cinder Shrike observes from concealment and retains the advantage of darkness.
Conduct
The Cinder Shrike is a nocturnal ambusher. Its attacks are defined by surprise and darkness. It favors conditions in which shape, distance, and movement cannot be judged with confidence. A darkened passage, roofline, hollow, or ruin may therefore conceal its approach without requiring any visible disturbance.
The creature’s sudden violence is the principal danger. Observers who identify the silhouette before an attack have not thereby established safety. The Cinder Shrike remains watchful until the instant of movement, then acts with abrupt force. Its silence prevents ordinary warning, while its cinder-dark appearance permits it to merge with soot, burned masonry, and other blackened surfaces.
Range Record
The Cinder Shrike lairs in Mournwatch. The record establishes Mournwatch as its lair, but does not authorize assumptions regarding the extent, number, or internal arrangement of such lairs. Search operations conducted in darkness are consequently judged unsound unless the conditions of concealment have been addressed.
Threat Assessment
Threat rating: 9.
This rating reflects the combined severity of the creature’s ambush habit, its reliance on darkness, and the extreme suddenness of its attacks. The rating is not reduced by the apparent inactivity of a suspected site. Silence is consistent with the creature’s documented demeanor.
Personnel encountering blackened, ember-dusted forms in Mournwatch are instructed to treat the observation as potentially significant. No attempt should be made to provoke movement merely to confirm identification. The Cinder Shrike is most dangerous when confirmation is sought under conditions it controls: at night, in obscurity, and without warning. Its defining traits are not ornamentation but operational hazards—shrike-like form, cinder aspect, silent vigilance, and violent suddenness.
Diadem of Sorrowgate
Identification
Diadem of Sorrowgate is a reliquary forged in 281 AS. Its recorded artifact class is reliquary. The object is housed in Gloammarch. Its forging site is Thorncairn, and the forging occurred in 281 AS.
The designation “diadem” describes the artifact’s formal identity, not a confirmed function beyond its classification as a reliquary. No additional function is entered in the surviving record. The object is to be catalogued by its full name: Diadem of Sorrowgate.
Appearance
Its visual identity is that of a reliquary bearing the name Diadem of Sorrowgate. The term “diadem” remains part of the established designation. No supplementary construction details are required for identification in the current register.
The artifact carries an atmosphere of sorrow and solemn possession. This demeanor is persistent enough to form part of its catalogued description, although it does not establish a measurable effect or determine the nature of any matter housed within it.
Attunement
Attunement to Diadem of Sorrowgate costs 9. The cost is assessed as a fixed entry of the artifact’s record. No additional conditions of attunement are preserved in this dossier.
Custodial Note
Diadem of Sorrowgate is housed in Gloammarch. Its presence should be treated as a matter of custody and classification, not as evidence of ownership, allegiance, or active deployment. The record confirms location only.
The artifact’s solemn character warrants controlled handling during inspection. Such handling is an administrative recommendation derived from its recorded atmosphere of sorrow and solemn possession; it does not constitute a stated magical property.
Summary
Diadem of Sorrowgate - artifact class: reliquary
Diadem of Sorrowgate - forged: 281 AS
Diadem of Sorrowgate - attunement cost: 9
Diadem of Sorrowgate forged at Thorncairn (in 281 AS)
Diadem of Sorrowgate housed in Gloammarch
Edge of Gloamreach
Volume: Codex Vaeloria II: Armory of Relics and Bestiary
Classification
Description
Edge of Gloamreach is a grimoire whose visual identity is defined by the name Edge of Gloamreach borne upon it. Its presentation suggests a shadowed, twilight-bound atmosphere. The impression is one of diminished light and enclosed secrecy, though the artifact’s classification remains strictly that of a grimoire.
The recorded attunement cost of Edge of Gloamreach is 46. This value is to be treated as an established requirement for formal attunement. No alternate cost is recognized in this codex.
Provenance
Edge of Gloamreach was forged at Blackford. The authoritative forging record states that Edge of Gloamreach - forged: 303 AS. It is likewise recorded that Edge of Gloamreach is housed in Blackford.
Edge of Gloamreach’s forged is 303 AS. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise. Such accounts possess no standing against the established record and are not to be used when dating the artifact, assigning it to a period, or assessing its provenance.
Registry Note
The artifact’s name, class, attunement cost, place of forging, housing, and forging year are the controlling entries:
Edge of Gloamreach - artifact class: grimoire
Edge of Gloamreach - attunement cost: 46
Edge of Gloamreach forged at Blackford
Edge of Gloamreach housed in Blackford
Edge of Gloamreach - forged: 303 AS
The designation “Edge” is part of the artifact’s proper name and does not alter its classification. No weapon category is implied by the designation. Likewise, the twilight-bound demeanor is a descriptive assessment of its visual identity and atmosphere, not a separate registry class.
Until a superior record supersedes the Blackford registry, Edge of Gloamreach is to be catalogued as a grimoire forged in 303 AS at Blackford, housed in Blackford, and requiring an attunement cost of 46.
Gauntlet of Sorrowfell
Artifact Class: Regalia Attunement Cost: 12 Forged: 391 AS Forging Site: Vharencrag Fortress Current Repository: Greyfell Citadel
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell is regalia of severe aspect, recognized by its formal bearing and its atmosphere of sorrow and grim authority. Its visual identity is that of regalia bearing the name Gauntlet of Sorrowfell. No ornamental interpretation supersedes this designation; the artifact is catalogued under its full and exact name.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell was forged at Vharencrag Fortress and is housed in Greyfell Citadel. These locations are fixed entries in the armory register. The repository designation does not alter the artifact’s class, and the forging site does not constitute a separate title or variant.
The attunement cost of the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell is 12. This cost is recorded without qualification. Prospective handlers are therefore to consult the applicable regalia protocols before attempting attunement. The artifact’s sorrowful demeanor is likewise an identifying characteristic, not a supplemental epithet.
The authoritative record states plainly: Gauntlet of Sorrowfell's forged is 391 AS. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise. Such accounts are rejected. The accepted forging date is 391 AS, and no competing date has standing in this codex.
The supplied record gives no further verified particulars concerning the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell’s construction, prior bearers, powers, or ceremonial employment. Accordingly, none are entered here as fact. Its status remains defined by the following established particulars: Gauntlet of Sorrowfell - artifact class: regalia; Gauntlet of Sorrowfell - attunement cost: 12; Gauntlet of Sorrowfell forged at Vharencrag Fortress; Gauntlet of Sorrowfell housed in Greyfell Citadel; and Gauntlet of Sorrowfell - forged: 391 AS.
In all inventories, custody ledgers, and attunement schedules, the exact name Gauntlet of Sorrowfell is to be retained. Variations based on popular accounts are non-authoritative.
Gravemaw Wyrm
The Gravemaw Wyrm is a grave-associated predator of exceptional aerial dominance. Gravemaw Wyrm - threat rating: 8. Its presence converts the open sky into a zone of immediate peril wherever it ranges. The creature does not require concealment to establish danger; its command of the air is itself sufficient.
Gravemaw Wyrm - habit: sky hunter. This designation is literal. The wyrm is adapted to hunting through the sky, where its vast body and pronounced maw form a silhouette suited to pursuit, descent, and capture. The visible outline is not merely imposing. It is the defining warning of a predator built to be recognized only after escape has become doubtful.
Morphology
The Gravemaw Wyrm possesses a vast wyrm-like form. Its maw is pronounced, giving the head a grave-devouring aspect even when viewed at distance. The body presents as a continuous hunting shape rather than a creature designed for concealment. Its silhouette is built for hunting through the sky, with the proportions of an aerial predator plainly expressed.
No ornamental interpretation is required. The association with death is inherent to its form and conduct.
Demeanor
The Gravemaw Wyrm is relentlessly predatory. It carries the cold inevitability of death from above, and its approach should be treated as a direct escalation of danger rather than as a passing atmospheric disturbance. Reports that describe it as patient, curious, or territorial are insufficient classifications; the established demeanor is relentless predation.
Lair Record
Gravemaw Wyrm lairs in Marrowwell Abbey. The site is therefore recorded as a lair, not merely as a sighting ground or occasional refuge. Any approach beneath the open sky must account for the possibility of aerial threat. The presence of the lair does not lessen the creature’s mobility; it identifies the point from which its range is maintained.
Field Assessment
Avoid exposure where concealment is unavailable. Do not mistake distance for safety. The wyrm’s principal advantage is vertical dominance, and its grave-associated nature should be considered a reliable indicator of its threat profile. Under codex classification, the Gravemaw Wyrm is not a lesser sky predator or a regional nuisance. It is a threat-rating 8 creature whose hunting domain is the air itself.
Lantern Moth Swarm
The Lantern Moth Swarm is a siege-breaker of serious threat. It operates as a collective rather than as a singular beast, bringing mothlike disruption against fortified positions. Its presence is best understood as an environmental assault: a dense cloud of moths occupies the air, the approaches, and the immediate visual field of those within the affected position.
The swarm carries the eerie visual impression of lantern-light. This appearance is not to be treated as a calm illumination. It is a shifting, obscuring radiance produced by the massed insects, rendering the cloud difficult to read and its boundaries difficult to determine. The effect is especially severe when the swarm presses against walls, gates, towers, or other fortified positions.
Its demeanor is restless, overwhelming, and difficult to escape. The collective does not present the measured movement of a disciplined formation. It gathers, breaks, reforms, and presses onward as a single disruptive presence. Observers should not assume that dispersal of one portion signifies the retreat of the whole. The swarm’s defining danger lies in its mass and persistence as a collective.
The Lantern Moth Swarm lairs in Ashreach. Its association with fortified sites is therefore recorded as a matter of habit, not as evidence that every manifestation originates within a fortress or settlement. The designation siege-breaker describes its established function against fortified positions.
The Lantern Moth Swarm was unleashed in The Leaden Accord. This event remains the principal deployment record attached to the creature in the present catalogue. The entry establishes use, not ownership, command, or cause; no such attribution is entered here.
Field Recognition
Dense cloud formation.
Mothlike constituent forms.
Eerie visual impression of lantern-light.
Restless and overwhelming movement.
Escape considered difficult once the collective has closed around a position.
Serious threat to fortified positions.
Assessment
The Lantern Moth Swarm is consequently catalogued as a creature whose danger derives from concentration, visual disruption, and pressure against defensive works. Its individual moths do not define the encounter. The swarm does.

Marsh Revenant
The Marsh Revenant is a siege-breaker, defined by its ability to shatter fortified resistance. It is not a guardian of walls, nor a creature properly contained by walls. Its presence turns defense into desperation. Where resistance has been arranged behind stone, timber, earthworks, or other fortification, the Marsh Revenant advances as a direct negation of that preparation.
The Marsh Revenant is a revenant of stagnant, hostile ground. Marsh-wet decay clings to its corpse-like figure, while its frame possesses the grim solidity of a breaker of walls. Its appearance suggests both burial and prolonged exposure to foul water: a body preserved without mercy, hardened without purpose, and burdened by the weight of the ground from which it arose. No ornament is required to identify it. Its mass, condition, and forward motion are sufficient.
Its demeanor is one of tireless, impersonal hostility. The Marsh Revenant does not threaten, negotiate, or display recognizable passion. It advances with the inevitability of the dead. Delay does not diminish its intent. Obstacles do not invite reconsideration. Its movement is therefore treated as a pressure upon the entire defensive position rather than as the approach of a single combatant.
Marsh Revenant - habit: siege-breaker
The Marsh Revenant lairs in Greyfell Citadel. The site is accordingly recorded as a place of military concern, regardless of the condition of its walls or the strength of its garrison. A defense confronted by the creature must be understood as already compromised in principle. The relevant question is not whether the structure can withstand an ordinary assault, but how long its defenders can maintain organized resistance while the Revenant advances.
For field identification, observers are instructed to distinguish the creature’s corpse-like form from ordinary remains by its purposeful motion and wall-breaking solidity. Stagnant decay alone is not sufficient evidence. The determining signs are the convergence of marsh-wet corruption, relentless advance, and the visible conversion of defensive confidence into desperation.
The accompanying numbered plate records the Marsh Revenant’s figures. Consult the plate for those measurements and other recorded values; they are not reproduced in this entry. Its operational significance is summarized here: the Marsh Revenant is encountered as a moving breach, a manifestation of hostile ground, and a persistent assault upon the idea that fortification guarantees safety.
Pale Stag of Omens
The Pale Stag of Omens is a burrowing horror of serious threat. Its title is not ornamental. The designation identifies two concurrent properties: its subterranean nature and the portentous impression carried by its presence. It is therefore catalogued as both a physical danger and an omen-bearing creature.
The Pale Stag of Omens appears as a pallid stag. Its antlered form is unmistakable, yet the animal resemblance does not lessen its horror. The antlers are the defining feature of its silhouette; the pallor of its body gives the creature a corpse-like aspect without rendering it inert or diminished. Observers consistently report that the form itself carries an unmistakable sense of omen.
Its demeanor is quiet. It does not require spectacle to inspire dread. The Pale Stag of Omens produces fear through quiet foreboding: the apprehension that its appearance signifies what may follow. This effect is considered intrinsic to the creature’s presence rather than dependent upon a declared threat or visible act.
The known lair of the Pale Stag of Omens is Hollowreach. The location is accordingly treated as a site of elevated concern. Any indication of subterranean movement, disturbed ground, or a pallid antlered outline within Hollowreach warrants classification as a possible manifestation of the creature. Such indications do not establish the creature’s presence by themselves.
The Pale Stag of Omens was unleashed in The Winter Reckoning. This event remains the principal recorded association attached to the creature in the current codex. The record establishes its release, but does not by itself define the full extent of the creature’s activity or subsequent whereabouts.
Its threat rating: 5 places it among serious hazards requiring disciplined assessment. The rating should not be interpreted as a measure of its omen, symbolism, or psychological effect. It records the creature’s standing as a danger; the dread produced by its quiet foreboding is a separate characteristic.
Field annotation: Avoid treating the Pale Stag of Omens as a conventional beast. Its stag-like appearance is certain, but its classification as a burrowing horror is equally certain. The pallid body, antlered form, subterranean habit, and portentous presence must be considered together.
Salt-Blind Leviathan
The Salt-Blind Leviathan is a creature classified as a siege-breaker of moderate threat. Its defining characteristics are immense destructive force and an inability to rely on sight. It does not present the aspect of a swift hunter or a calculating stalker. Its movement conveys ponderous, relentless pressure: a continuous advance that treats resistance as a condition to be endured rather than a barrier to be avoided.
The Salt-Blind Leviathan appears as a vast leviathan, its body marked by pale, salt-crusted features. Sightless eyes occupy the expected place upon its head, but provide no reliable faculty of perception. The creature is therefore defined not merely by blindness, but by the absence of sight as a meaningful dependence. Its conduct must be understood through pressure, disturbance, and the persistence of its advance rather than through visible attention or directed observation.
Its destructive force is immense. This force is expressed most characteristically against fortified resistance, where the creature’s mass and inexorable motion become instruments of breach. The designation siege-breaker describes its established habit, not a specialized weapon or a temporary condition. It is suited to the reduction of barriers by sustained impact and pressure. No account should treat its lack of sight as evidence of weakness. The Salt-Blind Leviathan remains dangerous precisely because its progress does not require ordinary visual certainty.
The creature’s demeanor is ponderous and relentless. It does not convey panic, haste, or deliberation in familiar proportions. Instead, it imposes the impression of a burden moving under its own inevitable weight. Witnesses may perceive the approach as slow, but slowness must not be confused with hesitation. The creature’s pressure is the relevant measure: constant, difficult to redirect, and destructive when allowed to continue.
Salt-Blind Leviathan lairs in Greythrone. The lair designation establishes its recorded place of habitation and should be treated as the primary reference for assessments concerning its presence. Where the creature is identified, its inability to rely on sight and its immense destructive force are both operational concerns. Containment estimates must account for the creature’s vast scale, pale salt-crusted exterior, sightless eyes, and relentless siege-breaking habit.
Assessment: Salt-Blind Leviathan — threat rating: 4.
Plate - The Cinder-Wrought Aegis: consult the plate for the recorded figures.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis
Classification: Artifact Artifact class: regalia Forging site: Embermarch Current housing: Gloamreach Forged: 342 AS
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis is regalia shaped by the legacy of the Sundering. Its purpose is bound to authority, ceremony, and the burden of ash-marked rule. It is not catalogued as a weapon, implement, or vessel. Its significance lies in the office it represents and in the formal weight imposed upon those who would preserve, display, or invoke it.
The Aegis appears as imposing regalia worked in a cinder-dark style. Its surfaces suggest fire-scarred craftsmanship: severe planes, darkened finishes, and workmanship that presents damage as part of its intended dignity. No softness is attributed to its appearance. Its visual language is one of endurance beneath ruin.
Its demeanor carries an austere atmosphere of sovereignty endured beneath ruin. This quality is not described as ornament, illusion, or enchantment in the surviving register. It is a recognized impression produced by the artifact’s form, condition, and ceremonial purpose. The Aegis therefore belongs among relics whose authority is communicated through presence rather than ornament alone.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis was forged at Embermarch. It is housed in Gloamreach. These locations are retained as separate entries in the armory record and are not to be conflated. The place of forging establishes its origin; the place of housing establishes its recorded custody.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis's forged is 342 AS. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise. This correction is authoritative. Scribes are to preserve the date as 342 AS in inventories, ceremonial rolls, and citations concerning the artifact.
The accompanying numbered plate records the artifact’s figures and provides the proper visual reference for its documented proportions and features. Consult the plate when those recorded figures are required; the plate, rather than an unauthorised summary, is the controlling reference for that purpose.
In ceremonial contexts, the Aegis should be treated as a burden-bearing emblem of ash-marked rule. Its cinder-dark presentation does not lessen its authority. It defines that authority as something maintained beneath ruin, under the discipline of ceremony, and without any promise of comfort.
The Crown of Burned Names
Artifact class: ward Forged: 266 AS Attunement cost: 60 Forge-site: Hollowvale Current housing: Blackford
Classification
The Crown of Burned Names is a ward whose defining character lies in the tension between protection and the erasure carried by burned names. Its classification establishes its function as a protective artifact, but does not lessen the memorial quality imposed by its form or title.
The Crown of Burned Names was forged at Hollowvale in 266 AS. It is housed in Blackford. These locations are entered as separate points of record: Hollowvale is the forge-site, while Blackford is the present housing site.
Attunement cost is 60. The cost reflects the burden of establishing a guarded identity in the presence of names that have been burned away. No lesser designation is recognized for partial attunement.
Appearance
The Crown of Burned Names is a crown of blackened, name-scarred material. Its silhouette is stark and funerary. The surface bears the visible consequence of burned names rather than a polished declaration of rank. The object should therefore be read first as a ward of remembrance and guarded identity, and only second as a crown.
The material is described by its blackening and scars. The scars are integral to its identification. Removal, concealment, or alteration of those marks would compromise the artifact’s recognizable presentation, though the dossier assigns no separate mechanism to such treatment.
Demeanor
The Crown of Burned Names imposes a hushed atmosphere of remembrance, loss, and guarded identity. This atmosphere is a persistent aspect of the artifact’s demeanor. It is neither celebratory nor openly martial. Its presence favors restraint, silence, and the careful preservation of what remains identifiable.
The ward’s protective identity is therefore inseparable from erasure. The burned name is not merely absent; it is carried as a mark. The crown offers no simple distinction between defense and mourning. Its authority derives from that unresolved condition.
Registry Note
The Crown of Burned Names is to be catalogued under ward, with its funerary silhouette and name-scarred material retained as primary identifiers. Its recorded history begins with its forging at Hollowvale in 266 AS and continues through its housing in Blackford.
The Hollow Edge
Artifact Class: ward Forged: 216 AS Forged at: Hollowvale Housed in: Crookgate Keep Attunement Cost: 21
Classification
The Hollow Edge is a ward forged in 216 AS. Its classification is fixed as ward. The record assigns no alternate class, derivative designation, or subordinate form. In catalogues, the article is entered under its full name: The Hollow Edge.
Its visual identity is that of a ward bearing the name The Hollow Edge. This distinction is descriptive rather than interpretive. The appearance establishes recognition in inventories and examination chambers; it does not, by itself, establish the extent or nature of the ward’s operation.
Provenance
The Hollow Edge was forged at Hollowvale in 216 AS. This place and year constitute its recorded forging provenance. The dating is expressed in the calendar of the Ashen Era and is not to be converted into an alternate reckoning.
The artifact is housed in Crookgate Keep. Housing is the recorded custodial condition of The Hollow Edge. It should not be confused with the place of forging: Hollowvale is recorded as the site at which the ward was forged, while Crookgate Keep is recorded as the site in which it is housed.
Attunement
Attunement to The Hollow Edge costs 21. The value is entered without supplementary measure. Any claimant, bearer, or examiner consulting the armory register must account for this cost before attempting attunement.
Demeanor
The Hollow Edge suggests an atmosphere of emptiness and severity. This demeanor is consistently associated with its catalogued presence. It is not described as warmth, abundance, or ease. The impression remains austere: an absence made perceptible, bounded by the strict visual identity of a ward.
The Hollow Edge is therefore indexed by four controlling particulars: its class as a ward, its forging at Hollowvale in 216 AS, its attunement cost of 21, and its housing in Crookgate Keep. These particulars define the artifact’s established entry in Codex Vaeloria II: Armory of Relics and Bestiary.
The Psalter of Seven Sorrows
Artifact Record
The Psalter of Seven Sorrows is a ward forged in 119 AS. Its artifact class is ward. The recorded place of forging is Ironfell Citadel, and the forging occurred in 119 AS. The artifact is housed in Fenthrone.
Attunement to The Psalter of Seven Sorrows costs 49. No alternate cost, classification, or forging record is entered in this volume.
Appearance
The Psalter of Seven Sorrows presents the visual identity of a ward bearing the name The Psalter of Seven Sorrows. Its designation is not supplementary to its appearance; the named identity is part of the artifact’s recorded presentation. Examination is therefore to distinguish the ward as catalogued, without assigning an unrecorded shape, material, ornament, or mechanism.
Demeanor
The Psalter of Seven Sorrows carries an atmosphere of sorrow shaped by its name. This quality is catalogued as demeanor rather than as a measured effect. The record establishes the presence of sorrow in the artifact’s character, but does not assign a separate manifestation, duration, target, or range.
The term “Psalter” is retained as part of the artifact’s exact name. It does not alter the artifact class. The Psalter of Seven Sorrows remains a ward, and its attunement cost remains 49.
Custody and Provenance
The registered provenance is concise: The Psalter of Seven Sorrows was forged at Ironfell Citadel in 119 AS and is housed in Fenthrone. These entries are distinct. Ironfell Citadel is recorded as the place of forging; Fenthrone is recorded as the place of housing.
No further transfer, bearer, keeper, construction method, material, or operative capacity is entered under this artifact. Such matters are outside the surviving record and are not to be supplied by inference.
Catalog determination: The Psalter of Seven Sorrows is a ward of sorrowful demeanor, forged at Ironfell Citadel in 119 AS, housed in Fenthrone, and requiring an attunement cost of 49.
The Sceptre of Final Winter
Artifact Class: ward Forged: 87 AS Forge-Site: Emberdeep Current Housing: Palewell Abbey Attunement Cost: 55
The Sceptre of Final Winter is a ward forged at Emberdeep in 87 AS. Its present housing is Palewell Abbey. These particulars constitute the accepted registry record; no alternate forge-site or housing is recognized in the relevant entries.
The object’s visual identity is that of a ward bearing the name The Sceptre of Final Winter. Its form is therefore to be read as an instrument of designation as much as an implement of use. The name is not ornamental in the catalogue sense: it is the identifying mark by which the artifact is distinguished from other wards.
Its demeanor is equally explicit. The Sceptre of Final Winter radiates an atmosphere of cold finality. This quality is perceptible without requiring any additional interpretation of the ward’s construction. It is the principal environmental impression associated with the artifact and remains the standard description used in formal inventories.
Attunement to The Sceptre of Final Winter costs 55. The cost is recorded as a fixed requirement of the artifact and is not to be conflated with its classification as a ward. No additional attunement conditions are entered in this volume.
The forging record is likewise fixed: The Sceptre of Final Winter - forged: 87 AS. The associated place is Emberdeep, giving the complete entry as follows: The Sceptre of Final Winter forged at Emberdeep (in 87 AS). The housing record is separate and current in function: The Sceptre of Final Winter housed in Palewell Abbey.
For catalogue purposes, the artifact should be cited under its full name. Abbreviated references may obscure its identity and are unsuitable for transfer records, attunement ledgers, or ward inventories. The accepted designation remains The Sceptre of Final Winter, with artifact class ward, forging year 87 AS, attunement cost 55, forge-site Emberdeep, and housing Palewell Abbey.
The Silent Psalter
The Silent Psalter is an instrument forged in 204 AS, at Fenspire. Its present housing is Marrowwatch. These particulars are sufficient for formal identification; no supplementary title or alternate designation is recognized in the catalogue.
Though made for expression, The Silent Psalter is defined by silence. Its construction provides no ordinary promise of song, proclamation, or release. Instead, the artifact imposes a grave discipline upon any wielder who seeks to establish attunement. The required attunement cost is 49. This cost is not treated as incidental notation. It is the principal measure by which the Psalter’s burden is assessed.
The artifact resembles a somber devotional instrument. Its form is muted and visibly fashioned for silent use. Surfaces, fittings, and resonant elements present no theatrical ornamentation. The whole is arranged toward restraint rather than display. Whether held, prepared, or set aside, The Silent Psalter maintains the visual character of a thing intended to contain expression rather than produce it.
Its demeanor evokes restrained sorrow and an oppressive quiet that resists release. This quality is persistent. The Psalter does not merely lack sound; it conveys the pressure of sound withheld. Observers commonly describe its presence in terms of diminished breath, closed recitation, and discipline maintained beyond comfort. Such descriptions are classificatory impressions, not evidence of an audible effect.

Its outline may seem near at one instant and remote at the next. Such impressions should not be treated as evidence of ordinary movement. The form is bound to the conditions of perception under which it is observed, particularly when the observer is exhausted, sleeping, or emerging from sleep.

Ashreach presents the bleak, marsh-bound aspect of a settlement caught between ash and water: low structures stand above saturated ground, paths divide and vanish among dark pools, and the settlement’s visible limits are difficult to distinguish from the surrounding mire.
Ashreach is currently contested. It is ruled by The Bleeding Crown, but that rule does not render the holding secure. Authority is maintained under pressure, and the settlement remains exposed to interruption, challenge, and sudden change. The contested status is therefore a formal condition of Ashreach, not a temporary description of local unease.
The garrison strength of Ashreach is 2598. This makes Ashreach a defended but unsettled holding rather than a core stronghold. The garrison establishes a meaningful military presence, yet its number does not alter the settlement’s disputed character. Defensive readiness is visible throughout the holding, but permanence is not.
The atmosphere of Ashreach is tense, unstable, and perpetually threatened. Routine activity proceeds beneath the expectation of disruption. Marsh weather, standing water, and ashfall impose continual burdens on movement and maintenance. Such conditions reinforce the settlement’s defensive posture without resolving the question of its long-term security.
Ashreach - founded: 122 AS. This is the authoritative founding record. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise. Those accounts are incorrect and carry no standing against the established entry. Ashreach was founded in 122 AS.
Ashreach is accordingly classified as a contested holding of The Bleeding Crown within The Weeping Marshes. Its garrison strength of 2598 confirms defense; its atmosphere and status confirm instability. The settlement’s significance lies not in secure consolidation, but in its continued maintenance amid conditions that resist certainty.
Blackford
Blackford stands on The Pale Coast, where the coast’s pale severity gives the settlement its defining visual character. Its buildings, defenses, and exposed approaches present a stark and dark aspect. The effect is deliberate or merely inherited; the record does not distinguish between the two. Blackford is recognizable by its severity rather than by ornament, color, or civic display.
Blackford was founded in 159 AS. Its origin establishes an old claim, but not an uncontested one. The settlement remains a core location, while its political status is contested. These conditions coexist without resolution. Blackford is therefore treated as strategically significant, yet not as a place whose authority is universally accepted.
The garrison numbers 3065. Its presence gives Blackford a military character, but the settlement’s demeanor is not one of secure possession. It feels watchful and strained, as if every road, shoreline approach, and internal passage demands continued scrutiny. The garrison’s duty is consequently understood through defense as much as through display. Blackford is caught between military defense and unresolved conflict; neither condition can be treated as temporary by default.
Blackford is ruled by The Bleeding Crown. This rule is recorded as fact, while the contested status remains in force. The two entries should be read together: the identity of the ruler does not remove the dispute surrounding the settlement.
At close range, Blackford’s austerity is more evident than any civic grandeur. Dark surfaces and severe lines stand against the pale coast. The settlement appears built for endurance, observation, and refusal of easy approach. Weather may obscure its edges, but does not soften its reputation. Servants, soldiers, and residents conduct ordinary business under the pressure of a place that is continually required to demonstrate its value.
Gazetteer classification is therefore precise: Blackford is a core location of The Pale Coast, founded in 159 AS, garrisoned by 3065, and ruled by The Bleeding Crown. Its status is contested. Its appearance is stark and dark. Its prevailing demeanor is watchful and strained. All further assessments should preserve these distinctions.
Cindermere Hold
Cindermere Hold is a ruined fortress of The High Spires. It was founded in 246 AS, when the elevated reaches were still considered suitable for a permanent military work. Its position combines defensive height with severe exposure: the hold stands apart from ordinary settlement and access routes, its surviving structure reduced to a stark silhouette against the surrounding stone and sky.
The garrison of Cindermere Hold once numbered 8878. That figure records the scale of its former military establishment, not its present occupancy. The hold is now abandoned and is not a core holding. Its empty chambers, breached approaches, and unmaintained defenses provide no evidence of an active garrison.
In appearance, Cindermere Hold combines the blackened severity of cinders with the elevated isolation of the High Spires. Its walls retain the impression of disciplined construction, though weathering and neglect have altered their original surfaces. Dark masonry, broken towers, and high ledges form a profile that remains legible at a distance. The structure is therefore recognized less by habitation than by its imposing outline.
The hold’s demeanor is one of immense former strength hollowed into ruin. Its scale exceeds its current function. Heavy defensive works remain where they can, but their silence emphasizes the loss of the force that once occupied them. Empty parapets and roofless interior spaces convey endurance without recovery.
Administrative records place Cindermere Hold under The Ashen Vanguard. This designation concerns the hold’s ruling authority and does not change its abandoned status or its classification as not a core holding. The site remains a military relic within The High Spires: a fortress whose elevation has preserved its visibility, while its isolation has sharpened the impression of abandonment.
Cindermere Hold is consequently catalogued as a former stronghold rather than an active seat of power. Its importance derives from the contrast between its documented garrison strength of 8878 and its present condition. The surviving silhouette expresses that contrast without ambiguity: blackened severity, elevated isolation, and immense former strength hollowed into ruin.

Crookgate Keep
Crookgate Keep is a fortified location in the Weeping Marshes, founded in 294 AS. It stands beyond the realm’s core holdings and is classified as contested. The keep’s present rule is attributed to The Bleeding Crown. This ruling condition does not remove its contested status; both designations remain operative in the gazetteer.
The keep’s visual identity is inseparable from the bleak character of the Weeping Marshes. Its walls, towers, and enclosed approaches are read against wet ground, dim horizons, and the persistent severity of the surrounding landscape. The result is not an isolated architectural style, but a place whose appearance is defined by its setting. Crookgate Keep presents as a stronghold made severe by the marsh around it.
Its demeanor is correspondingly uncertain. The atmosphere of Crookgate Keep is marked by its contested status: authority is present, but the permanence of that authority is not treated as settled. Records therefore describe the keep through condition rather than confidence. It is held, but not regarded as secure; administered, but not removed from dispute. This uncertainty is a defining feature of the location and should be considered alongside its formal designation.
The keep’s position outside the realm’s core holdings further determines its gazetteer classification. Crookgate Keep is not entered among the central possessions of the realm. Its geographic separation and contested status are recorded as distinct conditions, neither replacing the other.

Crookvale
Crookvale is a highland settlement of The High Spires, founded in 295 AS. Its present structure is rebuilt, though the settlement has not been restored to the position of a core holding. Crookvale remains outside the core holdings and is ruled by House Morvain.
The settlement’s rebuilt structure bears a crooked, hard-edged identity suited to a highland settlement. Its lines, defenses, and clustered construction present no impression of softness or ease. Crookvale appears shaped by necessity rather than ornament. Angles dominate its visible profile, and the whole settlement conveys the impression of having been forced into continued use after destruction.
Its demeanor is wary and resilient. Crookvale behaves as though survival has become its governing principle. Access, stores, and defenses are treated as matters requiring scrutiny. Local custom favors endurance over display, and authority is most readily recognized when it demonstrates practical control. The settlement does not project confidence; it projects persistence.
The garrison of 1004 is the clearest expression of Crookvale’s present function. It is not merely a population center with defensive personnel attached. The garrison defines the settlement’s public posture, reinforcing its guarded character and maintaining the distinction between a secure approach and an exposed one. The record does not assign Crookvale a place among the core holdings; its significance instead rests upon its continued occupation and defense.
House Morvain’s rule is therefore visible through administration, discipline, and the maintenance of the rebuilt settlement. Crookvale’s crooked form should not be mistaken for disorder. Its irregularity is functional, and its severity is consistent with a community that has outlasted damage without abandoning caution.
For travelers, Crookvale is best understood as a settlement of controlled access and limited assurance. Its inhabitants are wary, its defenses are maintained, and its rebuilt character remains evident in every hard-edged line. The settlement offers endurance rather than welcome, and continuity rather than comfort. In the records of The High Spires, Crookvale stands as a rebuilt holding whose governing principle is survival.

The fortress bears a scorched, crag-bound identity that contrasts with the broken landscape of the Shattered Vale. Embercrag Fortress was founded in 207 AS. Its establishment belongs to the recorded settlement history of The Shattered Vale, though the present ruin provides little indication of its former function beyond the fortress designation itself. Embercrag Fortress is ruled by The Silent Choir, whose authority remains the recognized ruling association for the location. The fortress’s appearance is inseparable from the scorched, crag-bound impression conveyed by its name. Against the broken landscape of The Shattered Vale, its ruin presents as a fixed remnant rather than a functioning seat of power. Emberdeep

Emberdeep is ruled by The Ashen Vanguard. This rule is to be understood as a claim of authority over an abandoned site outside the realm’s core holdings, not as evidence of a functioning settlement administration. No further institutional character is assigned in this entry.
The settlement’s visual identity is an empty habitation bearing the stark character of the Shattered Vale. Walls, lanes, and rooflines are present only as remnants or vacant forms; the site offers no reliable sign of ordinary continuity. Its condition is consistent with long neglect, though the codex assigns no additional cause beyond its recorded status.
The atmosphere of Emberdeep is silent and forsaken. Sound carries without answer. The absence of residents, trade, and visible administration is the defining condition of the site. Travelers should distinguish this silence from any formal declaration of neutrality: Emberdeep remains under the rule of The Ashen Vanguard, despite being abandoned and situated outside the realm’s core holdings.

Embermarch
Embermarch is a core location of the Gloaming Reach, established in 67 AS. Its recorded condition is garrisoned. The settlement presents the hardened visual identity expected of a garrisoned settlement in the Gloaming Reach: severe lines, controlled access, martial signage, and an arrangement governed by readiness rather than display.
Embermarch is ruled by The Ashen Vanguard. Its garrison strength is 4063. This figure defines the settlement’s military establishment in the current record and marks Embermarch as a position maintained for sustained vigilance. Personnel, stores, and defensive duties are organized according to the requirements of a permanent garrison.
The settlement’s demeanor is vigilant, martial, and prepared for danger. Civil arrangements are consequently subordinate to ordered defense. Movement through its approaches is controlled; routine activity bears the imprint of inspection, watch rotation, and readiness. Even in periods of calm, Embermarch does not present itself as a place at ease.
Its appearance is consistent with its role. Functional structures, hardened surfaces, and restrained ornament define the visible character of the settlement. Fires are maintained for use rather than ceremony. Equipment is kept accessible. Personnel are expected to remain responsive to summons and changes in condition. These qualities are not treated as temporary measures but as the ordinary expression of Embermarch’s garrisoned status.
The founding date of 67 AS places Embermarch within the post-Sundering record and establishes its earliest recognized entry in the gazetteer. No separate civic designation supersedes its military classification. In matters of authority, Embermarch is recorded under The Ashen Vanguard; in matters of regional placement, it belongs to the Gloaming Reach.
For travelers and officials, the principal identifying conditions are therefore clear: Embermarch is a core location, it is garrisoned, and it maintains a garrison strength of 4063. Its character follows directly from these entries. The settlement remains watchful, disciplined, and prepared for danger.
Fenspire
Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach, its silhouette defined by a stark spire rising above the dim character of the region. The structure is the settlement’s principal visual mark and its most immediate declaration of purpose. From the surrounding reaches, the spire presents a narrow, uncompromising profile against the muted sky.
Fenspire was founded in 57 AS. Its establishment belongs to the post-Sundering development of fortified holdings, though the settlement’s present condition is defined less by age than by function. Fenspire is a core location, maintained as a permanent military position rather than a transient camp or lightly held outpost.
The garrison consists of 3742 personnel. The garrisoned status is not nominal: military occupation shapes the settlement’s visible order, daily movement, and internal atmosphere. Patrols, watch rotations, secured approaches, and controlled access are defining conditions of Fenspire’s civic character. Civilian activity, where present, is conducted beneath this standing discipline.
Fenspire projects disciplined vigilance. Its atmosphere is shaped by permanent military occupation, and its architecture is read accordingly: walls, towers, gates, and enclosed ways are treated as instruments of observation and control. The settlement does not present itself as welcoming. It presents itself as prepared.
Fenspire is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel. Cartel authority is recorded as the settlement’s governing condition, while the garrison supplies the practical expression of that authority. Orders, provisions, inspections, and security measures therefore form the ordinary administrative texture of the location.
The term “Fenspire” is applied both to the settlement and to the dominant vertical structure that defines its appearance. In gazetteer usage, the distinction is resolved by context. References to the location indicate the whole fortified holding; references to the spire indicate the structure itself.
Fenspire remains a fixed, guarded presence within the Gloaming Reach: a settlement founded in 57 AS, garrisoned at 3742, and held under the rule of The Iron-Ring Cartel.
Fenthrone
Fenthrone is a fortified coastal seat on The Pale Coast, established in the aftermath of the Sundering’s altered order. Its visual identity is defined by walls, watch platforms, and pale coastal terrain. The settlement presents as a hard-edged installation rather than an open town: stonework and defensive structures stand against the stark pallor of the surrounding coast.
Fenthrone was founded in 229 AS on The Pale Coast. Its position remains outside the realm’s core holdings. No classification of the site as a core possession supersedes this status; Fenthrone is recorded as a separate coastal seat maintained under permanent military presence.
The settlement is garrisoned by 5805 troops. This strength governs the character of the place. Movement is observed, access is controlled, and ordinary activity proceeds beneath a standing discipline. The garrison is not merely an administrative detail: it is the settlement’s most immediate civic fact. Fenthrone feels watchful because it is watchful, with routines shaped by patrols, fixed posts, inspections, and the continual readiness expected of a fortified seat.
Fenthrone is ruled by The Bleeding Crown. Its allegiance is therefore entered in the gazetteer without qualification under that power’s authority. The designation does not alter the settlement’s geographic classification: Fenthrone remains a location on The Pale Coast, and it remains outside the realm’s core holdings.
Architecturally, the site favors defensive mass over ornament. Pale light, exposed stone, and the severe coastal setting reinforce the impression of a place built to endure scrutiny and pressure. The visual identity of Fenthrone is consequently inseparable from its garrisoned status. Towers, gates, and ordered approaches are read as signs of continued vigilance rather than ceremonial grandeur.
For purposes of regional accounting, Fenthrone should be cited by its full register: a garrisoned coastal seat of The Bleeding Crown, founded in 229 AS, holding 5805 troops, situated in The Pale Coast, and positioned outside the realm’s core holdings.
Gloammarch
Gloammarch stands in The Ash Wastes, where the land’s ash-dark austerity defines the settlement’s visible character. Its walls, towers, and public works present a bleak, martial aspect consistent with the name Gloammarch. Surfaces are commonly described in terms of soot, dust, and weathered stone; illumination, where maintained, serves practical purposes before ornamental ones. The settlement’s appearance is therefore not merely severe but administratively severe: every feature suggests endurance, vigilance, or the preservation of function under hostile conditions.
Gloammarch was founded in 321 AS. Its establishment places it among the recorded settlements of the Ashen Era, though no uncontested civic interpretation of its foundation is recognized in this entry. The settlement is a core location, a designation indicating strategic importance within the present territorial order. Its position in The Ash Wastes gives that designation particular weight, as control of the site remains a matter of active dispute.
Gloammarch is ruled by House Morvain. This rule is recognized in the settlement’s governing record, but the status of Gloammarch remains contested. The distinction is material: House Morvain exercises rule, while the wider claim to the settlement is not treated as settled. Official descriptions should retain both statements without substituting one for the other.
The recorded garrison strength is 2148. This force is the principal visible expression of Gloammarch’s martial condition and supports its continued holding as a core location. The garrison’s presence does not alter the settlement’s listed status. Gloammarch remains contested despite its garrison strength of 2148 and despite being ruled by House Morvain.
In demeanor, Gloammarch is tense and embattled. Its civic atmosphere is one of maintained readiness rather than confidence. Personnel, officials, and inhabitants are understood to conduct ordinary affairs under the pressure of persistent dispute. The settlement holds its ground amid that dispute; this is its defining civic posture.
For gazetteer purposes, Gloammarch should be recorded as a fortified core location of The Ash Wastes, founded in 321 AS, ruled by House Morvain, defended by a garrison strength of 2148, and retaining the status contested. Further claims regarding its jurisdiction, rivals, or future disposition are outside the certified record.
Gloamreach
Gloamreach is a core location on The Pale Coast, distinguished from the surrounding coast by its status as quarantined. Passage, commerce, and ordinary contact are consequently subject to guarded uncertainty. The settlement is not presented as an open coastal holding; its prevailing condition is one of enclosure and restriction.
The site bears the pallid, bleak visual character associated with The Pale Coast. Its structures, approaches, and exposed reaches carry the shadowed identity of the name Gloamreach. Light appears diminished there, whether by weather, architecture, or the apprehension of those who approach. This appearance is not ornamental. It reinforces the location’s sealed-off and ominous demeanor.
Gloamreach is ruled by House Morvain. Its garrison strength is 2483. This force is the principal visible measure of the location’s guarded condition, though the record does not reduce Gloamreach to a military station. Its quarantine and isolation define its public character as strongly as its walls, watch-posts, and controlled approaches.
The founding record is exact: Gloamreach's founded is 246 AS. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise. Such accounts are not accepted by this gazetteer and do not supersede the established date of 246 AS.
The location’s separation from the surrounding coast is therefore both administrative and perceptual. Gloamreach is marked by controlled distance: it stands within The Pale Coast, yet is set apart from it by quarantine. Visitors encounter not a conventional coastal settlement but a place whose boundaries are treated as consequential.

Its walls are best understood as remnants of a stronghold rather than as a functioning defensive installation. Towers, courts, and retaining structures may persist in partial form, but the site conveys no ordinary signs of occupation. Weathered surfaces, vacant approaches, and the absence of maintained standards reinforce its status.
Its former stronghold character has been reduced to abandonment. This distinction is material: Greyfell Citadel is not merely damaged, disused, or temporarily unoccupied. It is recorded as abandoned and lies outside the realm’s core holdings, where no central authority presently treats it as an active seat of power.

The ruin’s atmosphere is one of old desolation. Grey stone dominates the remaining profiles, while broken elevations and empty interior spaces mark the distance between its former purpose and its current condition. The site may therefore be used as a landmark of diminished sovereignty: a place where the architecture of rule survives after rule itself has withdrawn.

The stronghold’s visual identity is unmistakable. Grey walls and elevated defensive masses rise from the Gloaming Reach in the form of a throne, giving the location its name and its prevailing impression. The structure appears less constructed than imposed upon the surrounding land: a seat of rule rendered in stone, ash-coloured masonry, and severe angles. Its silhouette is intended to communicate endurance, command, and refusal of surrender.
Greythrone is garrisoned by 4672 troops. This force constitutes the principal visible instrument of order within the stronghold. Greythrone is ruled by The Ashen Vanguard. This designation records the governing power, not an uncontested settlement of all claims. The stronghold’s rule remains subject to constant pressure, and its administrative posture is consequently defensive, formal, and alert. Orders are issued with the expectation of scrutiny. Access, movement, and declarations of allegiance are matters of practical concern.
The surrounding reach reinforces this condition. Greythrone does not present itself as a secure centre from which influence naturally radiates. It is an exposed seat of authority, held beyond the realm’s core holdings and surrounded by the political uncertainty characteristic of contested ground. Its walls provide position and protection, but not finality.

Hollowreach
Hollowreach lies in the Gloaming Reach, where the settlement’s presence is defined by restriction, silence, and maintained separation. Its condition is not incidental to its appearance: Hollowreach presents the stark visual identity of a quarantined settlement in the Gloaming Reach, with every visible aspect subordinated to containment.

The settlement’s boundaries are understood less as civic limits than as instruments of quarantine. Hollowreach is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel. This authority is recorded as administrative fact; the settlement’s sealed demeanor and regulated presentation are consistent with that condition. No competing claim is entered in the present gazetteer. The Cartel’s control does not make Hollowreach open or prosperous. It confirms only that the settlement is governed, monitored, and retained under an active state of quarantine.

The result is a place that appears to have withdrawn from the surrounding Reach without ceasing to belong to it.
The designation quarantined is therefore both a status and a defining condition. Hollowreach is not merely isolated by circumstance; its isolation is preserved as policy. The settlement’s identity is inseparable from the limits imposed upon it, and its stark appearance records those limits more clearly than any proclamation.

All three conditions contribute to the citadel’s established character: durable, inaccessible, and grimly self-contained within The Weeping Marshes.

Marrowwell Abbey feels grimly steadfast. Religious austerity governs its internal character, while military vigilance governs its external function. Devotion and defense are not treated as separate duties within the holding. Silence, watchfulness, and strict routine shape its daily operation. The garrison of 6656 confirms that the abbey is a major defended site, regardless of its exclusion from the category of core holdings.

It remains a vigilant stronghold in The Gloaming Reach, combining the disciplines of sanctuary and garrison under the rule of The Bleeding Crown.

Mournwatch is a guarded settlement in the Gloaming Reach. Activity is measured, observation is constant, and the settlement’s visible order is that of a place prepared to endure uncertainty. Mournwatch is ruled by The Bleeding Crown. Its status as a garrisoned settlement and its location outside the realm’s core holdings are both recorded without qualification. These classifications distinguish Mournwatch from an unguarded rural holding or an ordinary interior settlement. Ash is not incidental to Stormmarch’s appearance; it informs the settlement’s surfaces, outlook, and general aspect. The result is a place that appears constructed to resist both the surrounding wastes and the consequences of prolonged isolation.

This condition governs Stormmarch’s practical character. Strength is maintained, but not freely projected. The garrison remains beneath restriction, and the stronghold is sealed away from ordinary movement.
Stormmarch is also outside the realm’s core holdings. This distinction is administrative as well as geographic in effect: the settlement belongs to the contested remainder of the realm rather than to its central, regularly integrated territories. Its authority is therefore expressed through occupation and containment rather than through broad civic reach.
The prevailing demeanor of Stormmarch is severe and sealed. Military readiness is evident, yet access is controlled; the settlement’s power is held beneath quarantine rather than displayed through expansion. Its walls and garrison communicate persistence, while its isolation communicates danger or necessary restraint without resolving either condition.
For gazetteer purposes, Stormmarch should be treated as a quarantined stronghold of The Ashen Vanguard, founded in 71 AS and situated in The Ash Wastes. Its defining contradiction is fixed: it possesses a garrison strength of 9263, but remains outside the realm’s core holdings and subject to continued quarantine.

The fortress presents a mountainous identity consistent with its location. Its appearance is severe, elevated, and shaped by the crags surrounding it. The resulting impression is one of force constrained by hostile terrain: a massive military position standing against conditions that permit no weakness. In disposition, Vharencrag feels formidable yet threatened.
The fortress’s founding in 84 AS places it among the established works of the post-Sundering realm. Its age is recorded, but its current condition is defined less by antiquity than by continued contention. The High Spires provide the setting; The Silent Choir provides the ruling authority; the garrison of 9478 provides the principal measure of its defended strength.
Gazetteer assessment: Vharencrag Fortress is a contested core location in the High Spires, founded in 84 AS, ruled by The Silent Choir, and maintained by a garrison strength of 9478. These details are expressions of its established status, not evidence of any separate civic rank.
Vharenford is ruled by The Ashen Vanguard. Governance and garrison function therefore present as a single visible order within the settlement. Instructions are expected to carry military weight, and readiness governs the settlement’s public demeanor. Its atmosphere is fortified and watchful. Even in periods without an identified disturbance, Vharenford conveys the expectation that its defenses must remain prepared.
The settlement’s hardened appearance is consistent across its principal aspects. Materials, structures, and maintained positions are understood through their utility. Ornament is secondary to endurance; access is secondary to control; and daily activity is measured against the needs of a garrisoned site. The Ash Wastes provide the setting, while the military establishment supplies Vharenford’s defining discipline.
For gazetteer purposes, Vharenford should be treated as a stable core location whose identity rests on three fixed conditions: its foundation in 291 AS, its status as garrisoned, and the presence of a garrison strength of 3637. These conditions distinguish it from an unoccupied ruin or a merely fortified waystation. Vharenford is a settled military presence under the rule of The Ashen Vanguard, marked by fortification, vigilance, and continuous preparation.

Conduct
The Choir is quiet, inscrutable, and deliberate in its handling of
truth. Statements are measured. Omissions are consequential. Disclosure
is treated as an act requiring the same care as inscription. The
faction’s silence is therefore not an absence of policy; it is a method
of policy.
Its custodians maintain a severe distinction between what may be
preserved, what may be concealed, and what may be rewritten. The

distinction is administered through religious authority rather than
public consent. For this reason, the Choir’s records possess both
archival and doctrinal weight.

the persistence of violence after formal hostilities had ended.

Operational Character
The war’s visual identity is one of blood-marked watchfulness,
exhausted armies, and an enemy line breaking under prolonged vigilance.
Its imagery is therefore defined less by sudden triumph than by the
persistence of forces that remain at their stations until opposition
fails.
The conflict feels brutal and decisive on the surface. Its recorded
outcome supports that appearance: the aggressors were totally routed,
and The Bleeding Crown received the formal victory. This conclusion is
not, however, a complete account of the war’s conduct.
Concealed Determinant
The secret truth of the War of Endless Vigil is that the losing
commander was bribed to withdraw. The withdrawal remains the concealed
determinant behind the apparent final collapse. Accordingly, the war is
classified as both a decisive rout and a corrupted victory.
This distinction is preserved in the annals without altering the
official result. The Bleeding Crown remains the recorded victor. The
total rout of the aggressors remains the recorded outcome. The hidden

payment does not nullify either entry; it qualifies the means by which
the conclusion was reached.
The casualty figure is recorded as 81577. The devastation of Crookvale,
the devastation of Thorncairn, and the fighting at Hollowreach
establish the war’s material imprint across its listed sites. Together
with the concealed bribery, these records define the conflict as an
episode of prolonged vigilance, exhaustion, betrayal, and final
collapse.
